title: Bless the Lord, O my soul (Psalm 102 [103])
hook: he knows we are dust, and his mercy is from eternity

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Invitatory, the psalm that opens every day of the Church's prayer. Your line was today, if you hear. What did you let in? Today, a psalm that talks to itself. Day one hundred seventy-seven.

Have you ever talked to yourself out loud? Come on. You can do this. Don't forget your keys. Most people do it, usually under their breath, usually in the car or the kitchen. It's how you get your own attention. The psalms do it too. Several times the one praying stops talking to God and turns to talk to their own soul, like giving yourself a nudge. And one psalm does nothing else in its opening lines. It's a pep talk to the self, and the subject is gratitude.
screen: `COME ON. YOU CAN DO THIS.` → `TALKING TO YOUR OWN SOUL.` → `A PEP TALK FOR GRATITUDE.`

segments.voice: Psalm 102 in the Douay, 103 in most Bibles: "Bless the Lord, O my soul: and let all that is within me bless his holy name. Bless the Lord, O my soul, and never forget all he hath done for thee." The Hebrew word for soul here, nephesh, doesn't mean a ghostly inner part. It means your whole living self, even your throat, your breath. So: all of me, wake up and remember. Why does the soul need reminding? Because we forget good things fast. The psalm makes a list: he forgives, he heals, he redeems your life from destruction, he crowns you with mercy, he renews your youth like an eagle's. Then it says the most tender things about God in the whole psalter. "As far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our iniquities from us." East and west never meet; you can walk forever and never reach where your sins went. "As a father hath compassion on his children, so hath the Lord compassion on them that fear him: for he knoweth our frame. He remembereth that we are dust." He remembers we're dust. Not to shame us, but to go easy on us. Then our shortness again, like the psalm of Moses: "Man's days are as grass." A wind passes over the flower and it's gone. "But the mercy of the Lord is from eternity and unto eternity upon them that fear him." The flower is short. The mercy isn't. And at the very end, the psalm turns outward: angels, heavenly hosts, all his works everywhere, bless the Lord. Then it comes home to where it began: bless the Lord, O my soul.
screen: `NEPHESH: YOUR WHOLE LIVING SELF.` · `AS FAR AS THE EAST FROM THE WEST.` · `HE REMEMBERETH THAT WE ARE DUST.` · `THE FLOWER IS SHORT, MERCY ISN'T.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name three good things. Settle, and breathe. Talk to yourself a little, the way the psalm does: come on, soul, remember. Then find three good things from the past few days. Not big ones. A meal, a text from a friend, a moment of sun, a thing that didn't go wrong. Name each one slowly and stay with it for a few breaths. If you pray, you can thank God for each: bless the Lord, O my soul. If you don't, let each one land fully before moving on. The bell holds the time.
Bless the Lord. The psalm's call to your whole self to remember, and to thank God, who knows we are dust. Today's word.
Your line: forget not his benefits. Tonight, before sleep, name the three good things again, and add one more from today. Day one hundred seventy-seven.

howItsDone: Catholics pray Psalm 102 [103] in the Liturgy of the Hours and hear it often at Mass as a responsorial psalm of mercy, with the refrain drawn from its line that the Lord is kind and merciful.

original.note: Hebrew: bless, O my soul, the psalm's opening words.

trapdoor: what you thought: a general hymn of praise.
what it means: a person talking to their whole self: remember the good, and thank the God who knows we are dust.
what a scholar hears: nephesh first meant throat or breath, then the whole living person; the psalm opens and closes with the same line to the soul.
